much.e: From Middle English muche (“much, great”), apocopated variant of muchel (“much, great”), from Old English myċel, miċel (“big, much”), from Proto-West Germanic *mikil, from Proto-Germanic *mikilaz (“great, many, much”), from Proto-Indo-European *meǵh₂- (“big, stour, great”).

muck.e: From Middle English mok, muk, from Old Norse myki, mykr (“dung”) or less likely Old English *moc, *moce (in hlōsmoc (“pigsty dung”) and lustmoce (“lady's smock (Cardamine pratensis)”)) (compare Icelandic mykja and Danish møg ("dung")), from Proto-Germanic *mukį̄ (“dung; manure”), from Proto-Germanic *muk-.

mud.e: From Middle English mud, mudde, mode, probably a borrowing from Middle Dutch mod, modde or Middle Low German mudde, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *mud-, *mudra- (“mud”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *mū-, *mew- (“moist”). Alternative etymology suggests the Proto-Germanic word is possibly borrowed from a Uralic language (compare e.g.
mud.g: A mixture of water and soil or fine grained sediment.

mud.e: From Dutch mud, from West Germanic, from Latin modius.
mud.g: A traditional Dutch unit of dry measure of variable size, frequently about 3 bushels.

muddle.e: From Middle English modelen (attested in present participle modeland (“wallowing”)), from Middle Dutch moddelen (“to make muddy”), from modde, mod (“mud”) (Modern Dutch modder). By surface analysis, mud + -le.
muddle.g: To mix together, to mix up; to confuse.

muddy.e: Mud, mudde is possibly borrowed from Middle Dutch modde, and/or Middle Low German modde, mudde, from Proto-Germanic *mud-, *mudra- (“mud”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *mū-, *mew- (“moist”). The English word is analysable as mud + -y (suffix meaning ‘having the quality of’ forming adjectives).
muddy.g: Covered or splashed with, or full of, mud (“wet soil”).
The edible mud crab or mangrove crab (Scylla serrata).

muffle.e: From Middle English muflen (“to muffle”), aphetic alteration of Anglo-Norman amoufler, from Old French enmoufler (“to wrap up, muffle”), from moufle (“mitten”), from Medieval Latin muffula (“a muff”), of Germanic origin (—first recorded in the Capitulary of Aachen in 817 C.E.).
muffle.g: Anything that mutes or deadens sound.

mulberry.e: From Middle English mulbery, molberye, murberie, partly from Old English mōrberġe (“mulberry”) (q.v.), and probably partly from Middle Low German mulbere (“mulberry”), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *mūrubaʀi ~ *mōrubaʀi, from Latin mōrus + Proto-West Germanic *baʀi.
mulberry.g: Any of several trees, of the genus Morus, having edible fruits.

mule.e: From Middle English mule, from Anglo-Norman mule (“she-mule”) and Old English mūl, both ultimately from Latin mūlus, from Proto-Indo-European *mukslós.
mule.g: The generally sterile male or female hybrid offspring of a male donkey and a female horse.

mule.e: From Middle French mule (“backless slipper”), from Medieval Latin mula (“slipper, shoe with a thick sole”), presumably from classical Latin mulleus, the dyed shoe of either the patricians or senators, from mūllus (“red mullet”) + -eus (“-y: forming adjectives”), from Ancient Greek μύλλος (múllos).
mule.g: Any shoe with an upper covering the front of the foot but without a back flap or strap, leaving the heel exposed.

mules.e: From the surname of the procedure's inventor, John Mules.
mules.g: To remove skin from (an animal) to prevent myiasis.

multiplication.e: Borrowed from Middle French, from Old French multiplicacion, from Latin multiplicatio, multiplicationem; ~equivalent to multiplicate + -ion.
multiplication.g: The process of computing the sum of an addition with one and the same number a specified number of times (i.e. 4 times 5 = [0 +] 5 + 5 + 5 +

multiply.e: From Old French multiplier, from Latin multiplicō, from multi (“many”) + plicō (“to fold”). The noun presumably derives from the verb.
multiply.g: To increase the amount, degree or number of (something).
Having more than one ply or layer; multilayered.

multitude.e: From Middle English multitude, multitud, multytude (“(great) amount or number of people or things; multitudinous”), borrowed from Old French multitude (“crowd of people; diversity, wide range”), or directly from its etymon Latin multitūdō (“great amount or number of people or things”), from multus (“many.
multitude.g: A great amount or number, often of people; abundance, myriad, profusion.

munition.e: From Latin mūnitiō (“a defence, fortification”) via French munition, from mūnīre (“fortify, defend (with a wall)”) + -tiō, from moenia (“city walls, defensive walls, or walls in general”). Equivalent to munite + -ion.
munition.g: Materials of war: armaments, weapons and ammunition.

murder.e: From Middle English murder, murdre, mourdre, alteration of earlier murthre (“murder”) (see murther), from Old English morþor (“secret slaying, unlawful killing”) and Old English myrþra (“murder, homicide”), both from Proto-West Germanic *morþr, from Proto-Germanic *murþrą (“death, killing, murder”), from Proto-Indo-European *mr̥tro- (“killing”).
murder.g: An act of killing a person unlawfully, especially with predetermination.

murderer.e: From Middle English murderere; equivalent to murder + -er.

murderous.e: From murder + -ous (suffix forming adjectives from nouns denoting possession or presence of a quality).
murderous.g: Of, characterized by, or pertaining to murder or murderers.

murmur.e: From Middle English murmur, murmor, murmour, from Old French murmure (modern French murmure), from Latin murmur (“murmur, humming, muttering, roaring, growling, rushing etc.”).
murmur.g: Any low, indistinct sound, like that of running water.

murrain.e: The adjective and adverb are derived from the noun.
murrain.g: Infectious disease; pestilence, plague; (countable) sometimes used in curses such as a murrain on someone: an outbreak of such a disease; a

muscle.e: From Middle English muscle, muscule, muskylle, and in part from Middle French muscle, from Latin mūsculus (“a muscle”, literally “little mouse”) because of the mouselike appearance of some muscles, from mūs (“mouse”).
muscle.g: A contractile form of tissue which animals use to effect movement.

muse.e: From Middle French muse, from Latin Mūsa, from Ancient Greek Μοῦσα (Moûsa).
muse.g: Of a person: a source of inspiration.

muse.e: From Middle English musen, from Old French muser.
muse.g: To become lost in thought, to ponder.

music.e: From Middle English musik, musike, borrowed from Anglo-Norman musik, musike, Old French musique, and their source Latin mūsica, from Ancient Greek μουσική (mousikḗ), from Ancient Greek Μοῦσα (Moûsa, “Muse”), an Ancient Greek deity of the arts. By surface analysis, muse + -ic (“pertaining to”).
music.g: A series of sounds organized in time, usually employing some combination of harmony, melody, rhythm, tempo, timbre, sound design, lyrics, et

musical.e: From Middle English musical, from Old French, from Medieval Latin mūsicālis, from Latin mūsica (“music”) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives); equivalent to music + -al.
musical.g: Of, belonging or relating to music, or to its performance or notation.

musician.e: From Middle English musician, musicien, from Old French musicien (“musician”), equivalent to musike + -ien. By surface analysis, music + -ician.
musician.g: A composer, conductor, or performer of music; specifically, a person who sings and/or plays a musical instrument as a hobby, occupation, or

must.e: From Middle English moste ("must", literally, "had to", the past tense of Middle English moten (“to have to”)), from Old English mōste (“had to”), 1st & 3rd person singular past tense of mōtan (“to be allowed, be able to, have the opportunity to, be compelled to, must, may”), from Proto-Germanic *mōtaną.
must.g: To do as a requirement; indicates that the sentence subject is required as an imperative or directive to execute the sentence predicate, wit

must.e: From Middle English must, from Old English must and Old French must, most, both from Latin mustum.
must.g: The property of being stale or musty.

mustard.e: From Middle English mustard, from Old French moustarde (French moutarde), from moust (“must”), from Latin mustum. Sometimes mistakenly thought to come from Latin mustum ardens, but such a Latin phrase is not attested, and it is well understood that that the final -ard is derived from Old French -arde.
mustard.g: A plant of certain species of the genus Brassica, or of related genera (especially Sinapis alba, in the family Brassicaceae, with yellow flo

muster.e: From Middle English musteren, borrowed from Anglo-Norman mostrer, Middle French monstrer, moustrer (whence the noun monstre, which gave the English noun), from Latin mōnstrō (“to show”), from moneō (“to admonish”).

mute.e: From Middle English muet, from Anglo-Norman muet, moet, Middle French muet, from mu (“dumb, mute”) + -et, remodelled after Latin mūtus.
mute.g: Not having the power of speech; dumb.

mute.e: From Middle French muetir, probably a shortened form of esmeutir, ultimately from Proto-Germanic.

mutter.e: From Middle English muteren, moteren, of imitative origin.
mutter.g: A repressed or obscure utterance; an instance of muttering.

mutual.e: Borrowed from Middle French mutuel, from Latin mūtuus.
mutual.g: Having the same relationship, each to each other.

muzzle.e: From earlier muzle, musle, mousle, mussel, mozell, from Middle English mosel, from Old French musel, museau, muzeau (modern French museau), from Late Latin mūsus (“snout”), probably expressive of the shape of protruded lips and/or influenced by Latin mūgīre (“to moo, bellow”).
muzzle.g: The protruding part of an animal's head which includes the nose, mouth and jaws.
